erythrae.t: Ionian city on the peninsula facing Chios, home of a famous Sibyl and member of the twelve-city Ionian League.
erythrae.o: Erythrae stood on the coast of the peninsula opposite Chios, founded by tradition by Cnopus, a son of Codrus of Athens, with mixed settlers c. 1000 BCE. It joined the Ionian League and, as an early rival of Chios, fought several wars with the island.
erythrae.r: The Erythraean Sibyl, a prophetess of Apollo, gave the city renown. Erythrae was governed by aristocracies and later oligarchies and democracies, and sent eight ships to the Battle of Lade in 494 BCE. An Athenian decree of the 450s BCE imposed a democratic constitution and garrison on it as a Delian League member.
erythrae.e: Erythrae revolted from Athens in 412 BCE and later swung between Persian, Athenian and Macedonian influence. In the Hellenistic period it was a free city, allied to Rome from the war against Antiochus III, and passed into the province of Asia after 133 BCE.

erdini.t: People of north-western Ireland recorded by Ptolemy, usually placed around Lough Erne and linked by name with the Érainn.
erdini.o: The Erdini are named in Ptolemy's Geography of about 150, placed inland in the north-west of Ireland, usually located around Lough Erne in modern Fermanagh and neighbouring parts of Donegal. Their name is often compared with Erne and with the Érainn, a population group of early Irish genealogies.
erdini.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers, settlements or customs. The lakeland around Lough Erne was well suited to crannogs and cattle farming, and if the name link with the Érainn holds, they belonged to a widespread group that early Irish historians regarded as one of the ancient peoples of Ireland.
erdini.e: The Erdini do not reappear in any source. Their territory later fell within the lands of the Kingdom of Airgialla and the northern Uí Néill.

empire-of-thessalonica.t: Short-lived Greek empire founded when Theodore Komnenos Doukas of Epirus took Thessalonica in 1224 and claimed the Byzantine throne.
empire-of-thessalonica.o: Theodore Komnenos Doukas, ruler of the Despotate of Epirus, steadily conquered the Kingdom of Thessalonica and captured the city in 1224. Around 1227 he was crowned emperor by Demetrios Chomatenos, archbishop of Ohrid, challenging the Empire of Nicaea for leadership of the Byzantine world and preparing to march on Constantinople.
empire-of-thessalonica.r: Theodore ruled a realm stretching from the Adriatic to Thrace, with Byzantine court titles and administration, and quarrelled with Nicaea's patriarch over church authority. In 1230 he attacked Bulgaria but was defeated and captured by Ivan Asen II at Klokotnitsa and later blinded. His brother Manuel then ruled as a Bulgarian client.
empire-of-thessalonica.e: Theodore regained Thessalonica for his son John, who in 1242 had to accept the lesser title of despot from John III Vatatzes. In 1246 Vatatzes took Thessalonica from John's brother Demetrios, annexing it to the Empire of Nicaea.

electorate-of-cologne.t: The prince-archbishopric of Cologne, one of the seven electors, whose archbishops crowned German kings and ruled a long strip of the Rhineland.
electorate-of-cologne.o: Cologne had been an archbishopric since the 8th century. In 953 Otto I made his brother Bruno archbishop and also duke of Lotharingia, founding the temporal power of the see. Grants of counties and, in 1180, the Duchy of Westphalia after the fall of Henry the Lion made the archbishops major territorial princes.
electorate-of-cologne.r: The Golden Bull of 1356 confirmed the archbishop as one of the seven electors and arch-chancellor of Italy. After the citizens defeated Archbishop Engelbert II in 1262 and the Battle of Worringen in 1288, Cologne became a free city, and the electors moved to Bonn. The Wittelsbach family held the see from 1583 to 1761, building the palaces at Brühl and Bonn.
electorate-of-cologne.e: French revolutionary armies took the Rhineland in 1794, and the electorate was dissolved in 1803; Westphalia went to Hesse-Darmstadt and other lands to Nassau. After 1815 the territories became Prussian. Cologne Cathedral, begun in 1248, was completed in 1880.

eretria.t: Euboean city that helped found Greek colonies in Italy and the north Aegean, and whose support for the Ionian Revolt brought Persian destruction in 490 BCE.
eretria.o: Eretria grew on the south coast of Euboea, facing Attica, in the 8th century BCE, possibly succeeding the earlier settlement at Lefkandi. With Chalcis it was a pioneer of long-distance Greek trade, and their rivalry over the Lelantine plain became the Lelantine War.
eretria.r: Eretrians joined Chalcis in founding Pithekoussai and settled Methone in Macedonia and, by tradition, Corcyra before the Corinthians. It was ruled by aristocracies of horse-breeders. Eretria sent five ships to help Miletus in 499 BCE, sharing in the burning of Sardis. Its later theatre and gymnasium are among the best-preserved on Euboea.
eretria.e: Persia sacked Eretria in 490 BCE and deported its people. Rebuilt, it joined the Delian League and later hosted the philosopher Menedemus. Rome sacked it in 198 BCE, and it lost independence in 146 BCE.
eretria.re: Greek religion; cult of Apollo Daphnephoros

estado-novo-portugal.t: Salazar's authoritarian New State, one of Europe's longest-lived dictatorships, which fought to keep Portugal's African empire.
estado-novo-portugal.o: The constitution of 1933, approved by plebiscite, turned the Ditadura Nacional into a corporatist regime under prime minister António de Oliveira Salazar, inspired by Catholic social teaching and the idea of an organic nation.
estado-novo-portugal.r: The regime banned parties except the National Union, censored the press and used the PVDE, later PIDE, secret police and the Tarrafal prison camp against opponents. Portugal stayed neutral in the Second World War, leased the Azores to the Allies and joined NATO in 1949. Its economy remained poor, prompting mass emigration, while from 1961 it fought costly colonial wars in Angola, Mozambique and Guinea-Bissau.
estado-novo-portugal.e: Marcelo Caetano succeeded Salazar in 1968 but failed to end the wars. On 25 April 1974 the Armed Forces Movement overthrew the regime in the Carnation Revolution, founding the Third Portuguese Republic.

elisyces.t: Iberian-influenced people of the coastal plain around Narbonne, among the first inhabitants of Gaul named in Greek writing.
elisyces.o: Known only from a handful of Greek sources. Hecataeus of Miletus names them around 500 BCE, and Herodotus lists Elisyces among the mercenaries hired by Carthage for the Battle of Himera in Sicily in 480 BCE. They held the Languedoc coast between the Pyrenees and the Hérault, with Naro, the oppidum of Montlaurès beside Narbonne, as their main centre.
elisyces.r: Archaeology suggests a mixed culture with strong Iberian features: Iberian script on pottery and lead tablets, fortified hilltop settlements such as Ensérune, and busy exchange with Greek Massalia and Emporion in wine, painted pottery and metals.
elisyces.e: The name fades from the record by the 3rd century BCE, when Celtic Volcae dominated the region. In 118 BCE Rome founded the colony of Narbo Martius next to Montlaurès, which became the capital of Gallia Narbonensis.

elis.t: City-state of the north-western Peloponnese that controlled the sanctuary of Olympia and organised the Olympic Games.
elis.o: Elis occupied the fertile lowlands of the Peneios in the north-western Peloponnese, settled by north-west Greek speakers in the early Iron Age. For centuries its people lived in villages; the Eleans won control of the sanctuary of Olympia from Pisa in the 6th century BCE, and the city of Elis was formed by synoecism in 471 BCE.
elis.r: Elis supervised the Olympic Games through officials called Hellanodikai, and its territory was regarded as sacred during the festival. It had an aristocracy and later a democracy, and its land produced horses and flax. Elis produced the sophist Hippias and the sceptic philosopher Pyrrho.
elis.e: Sparta defeated Elis in a war c. 402 to 400 BCE and stripped it of Triphylia. In the Hellenistic period Elis allied with the Aetolian League before joining the Achaean League in 191 BCE, and passed under Rome in 146 BCE.
elis.re: Greek religion; cult of Olympian Zeus

emirate-of-bari.t: Short-lived Muslim emirate in Apulia, centred on the port of Bari, which raided southern Italy until Louis II took it in 871.
emirate-of-bari.o: Arab and Berber soldiers, some of them mercenaries hired by the warring Lombard princes, seized Bari around 847 under a leader named Kalfun. From this base on the Adriatic coast they extended control over much of Apulia.
emirate-of-bari.r: Under Mufarraj ibn Sallam and then Sawdan, the last emir, Bari sought recognition from the Abbasid caliph and became an emirate with a congregational mosque. It lived largely from raiding and the slave trade, attacking Lombard and Byzantine territory and monasteries, though Sawdan also dealt diplomatically with Christian neighbours, and a Jewish chronicle recalls him as a figure of learning.
emirate-of-bari.e: The Carolingian emperor Louis II besieged Bari for several years with Lombard allies and Byzantine naval help, taking the city in 871 and capturing Sawdan. The Byzantines occupied Bari in 876, and it became the capital of the Theme of Longobardia.

emporion.t: The Greek trading city of Empúries in Catalonia, founded from Massalia, where the Romans first landed in Iberia in 218 BCE.
emporion.o: Around 575 BCE Phocaean Greeks from Massalia (Marseille) set up a trading post on a small island at the mouth of the Fluvià, now Sant Martí d'Empúries. Its name means 'market'. A larger new town, the Neapolis, soon grew on the mainland shore beside a native settlement of the Indigetes.
emporion.r: Emporion was a self-governing Greek polis trading wine, oil and fine pottery for grain, metals and textiles from the Iberian interior. It coexisted closely with its Indigetan neighbours, and from the 5th century BCE minted silver drachms, later with a Pegasus design that Iberian mints copied. Strabo notes a temple of Ephesian Artemis, and a famous statue of Asclepius was found in its sanctuary.
emporion.e: Allied with Rome, Emporion was the landing point of Gnaeus Scipio in 218 BCE and of Cato in 195 BCE, when he crushed the revolt of the north-east. A Roman town grew beside it, and under Augustus the two merged as the municipium of Emporiae.

electorate-of-trier.t: The ecclesiastical principality of the archbishops of Trier, one of the seven electors of the Holy Roman Empire, stretching along the Moselle and Rhine.
electorate-of-trier.o: Trier had been an imperial capital in late Roman times and a bishopric since the 3rd century. In 898 King Zwentibold granted Archbishop Ratbod immunity and comital rights over the city, the basis of the archbishops' temporal power. Over the following centuries they built a territory along the Moselle from Trier to Koblenz.
electorate-of-trier.r: Archbishop Baldwin of Luxembourg, brother of Emperor Henry VII, consolidated the territory between 1307 and 1354. The Golden Bull of 1356 confirmed the archbishop as an elector and arch-chancellor for Gaul and Burgundy. The electors moved their residence to Koblenz and Ehrenbreitstein, and Trier kept the Holy Robe relic, exhibited to pilgrims.
electorate-of-trier.e: French revolutionary armies occupied the left bank of the Rhine in 1794. The last elector, Clemens Wenceslaus of Saxony, fled, and in 1803 the Reichsdeputationshauptschluss dissolved the electorate, its remaining eastern lands going to Nassau-Weilburg. After 1815 most of it became Prussian.

etruscan-league.t: Federation of twelve Etruscan city-states that met yearly at the sanctuary of Voltumna, more a religious union than a military alliance.
etruscan-league.o: By the 6th century BCE the leading cities of Etruria formed a group known to the Romans as the twelve peoples of Etruria. Its focus was the Fanum Voltumnae, a federal sanctuary near Volsinii, possibly at Campo della Fiera below Orvieto, where delegates met each spring.
etruscan-league.r: The list of members changed over time but usually included Veii, Caere, Tarquinii, Vulci, Volsinii, Clusium, Perusia, Cortona, Arretium, Volaterrae, Vetulonia or Rusellae, and Populonia. The annual gathering combined sacrifices, games and markets with political councils, and chose a federal leader whose powers were mainly ceremonial. It rarely acted together in war: Livy says it refused to help Veii against Rome.
etruscan-league.e: As Rome conquered the Etruscan cities one by one, the League lost all political weight, ending with the destruction of Volsinii in 264 BCE. Under the Empire a ceremonial league of fifteen peoples was revived with a praetor of Etruria, and the festival was still held in the 4th century CE.

ebusus.t: The Punic city of Ibiza, a Carthaginian stronghold whose vast necropolis and Tanit cult make it a key site for Phoenician civilisation in the West.
ebusus.o: Phoenicians had a small trading post at Sa Caleta on Ibiza in the 7th century BCE. According to Diodorus, the city of Ebusus was founded in 654 BCE on the bay of modern Ibiza town, and it soon came under the influence of Carthage.
ebusus.r: Ebusus became one of the most important Punic cities in the western Mediterranean, producing wine, oil, salt, purple dye and pottery, and minting coins showing the god Bes. The Puig des Molins necropolis contains thousands of tombs, and the cave sanctuary of Es Culleram was dedicated to Tanit. It controlled trade with the Balearic Islanders and recruited their slingers.
ebusus.e: Ebusus stayed loyal to Carthage through the Second Punic War, but afterwards made a treaty with Rome. After the Roman conquest of the Balearics in 123 BCE it was increasingly integrated, becoming a Roman municipium under Vespasian while keeping Punic culture for centuries.

euzkadi-1936-1937.t: The first Basque autonomous government, formed during the Spanish Civil War and defeated within a year, after the bombing of Guernica.
euzkadi-1936-1937.o: After the outbreak of the Spanish Civil War, the Second Spanish Republic granted the Basque Country a Statute of Autonomy in October 1936. José Antonio Aguirre of the Basque Nationalist Party was sworn in as first lehendakari under the oak of Guernica on 7 October 1936.
euzkadi-1936-1937.r: The government controlled only Biscay and part of Gipuzkoa. It raised its own army, issued money and passports, and protected the Catholic Church, unlike much of Republican Spain. Bilbao's industry and port were its base, defended by the fortified Iron Ring.
euzkadi-1936-1937.e: Franco's Army of the North attacked in 1937. German and Italian aircraft destroyed Guernica on 26 April 1937, and Bilbao fell on 19 June. Basque troops surrendered to the Italians at Santoña in August. The government went into exile, and Basque autonomy was restored only in 1979.

east-francia.t: The eastern Carolingian kingdom created at Verdun in 843, from which the Kingdom of Germany and the Holy Roman Empire developed.
east-francia.o: The Treaty of Verdun in 843 divided the Carolingian empire among the three sons of Louis the Pious. Louis the German received the lands east of the Rhine, together with Mainz, Worms and Speyer on its west bank. He ruled them from palaces such as Regensburg and Frankfurt, and in 870 the Treaty of Meerssen added much of Lotharingia.
east-francia.r: East Francia combined Franks, Saxons, Bavarians, Swabians and Thuringians, each with strong regional identities that grew into stem duchies. Kings moved between palaces and relied on bishops and great abbeys. Arnulf of Carinthia defeated the Vikings on the Dyle in 891 and was crowned emperor in 896, but Magyar raids devastated the kingdom after 900.
east-francia.e: When the last Carolingian, Louis the Child, died in 911, the nobles elected Conrad I of Franconia, then in 919 Henry the Fowler of Saxony. Henry's son Otto I defeated the Magyars at the Lechfeld in 955 and was crowned emperor in 962, a date usually taken as the start of the Kingdom of Germany within the Holy Roman Empire.
east-francia.la: Old High German, Old Saxon, Latin

enchelei.t: Illyrian people around Lake Ohrid, linked by Greek legend to the hero Cadmus, among the earliest Illyrian groups named in Greek sources.
enchelei.o: Greek writers from Hecataeus and Herodotus onward place the Enchelei, the 'eel people', near Lake Ohrid and the Drin valley. Myth said Cadmus and Harmonia came to rule them after leaving Thebes, and that their descendants ruled the Illyrians. Little beyond these mentions survives, and their origins are otherwise unknown.
enchelei.r: Known only from scattered Greek references, the Enchelei appear as a tribal people of the lake district around Lychnidus (Ohrid), whose fisheries probably gave them their name. Later authors seem to treat the Sesarethii as the same or a successor people.
enchelei.e: By the 4th century BCE their name fades, and the region around Lake Ohrid appears under the Dassaretae and within the sphere of Macedon and the Illyrian Kingdom.

ephesus.t: Ionian port city of the Temple of Artemis, one of the Seven Wonders, and later the capital of Roman Asia.
ephesus.o: Ionian settlers led, by tradition, by Androclus, son of Codrus of Athens, founded Ephesus near the mouth of the Cayster c. 1000 BCE, beside a native cult of a mother goddess. The Greeks identified her with Artemis, and her sanctuary became the city's focus. Ephesus was one of the twelve cities of the Ionian League.
ephesus.r: Ephesus prospered from trade between the Aegean and inner Anatolia. Croesus of the Kingdom of Lydia took the city c. 560 BCE, ousting the tyrant Pindarus, and paid for columns of the great marble Artemision. The philosopher Heraclitus lived there. Under the Achaemenid Empire and then the Delian League it kept its temple economy, with the sanctuary acting as a bank and place of asylum.
ephesus.e: The temple burned in 356 BCE and was rebuilt in grander form. Lysimachus moved the city to a new site c. 290 BCE. After Seleucid, Ptolemaic and Pergamene rule, Ephesus passed to Rome in 133 BCE and became the chief city of the province of Asia.
ephesus.re: Greek religion; cult of Artemis of Ephesus

earldom-of-ormond.t: The great Butler lordship of Kilkenny and Tipperary, for four centuries one of Ireland's most powerful Anglo-Irish dynasties and a loyal crown ally.
earldom-of-ormond.o: The Butlers descended from Theobald Walter, who came to Ireland with Prince John in 1185 and held the hereditary office of butler of Ireland. In 1328 James Butler became the first Earl of Ormond and was granted palatine rights over Tipperary.
earldom-of-ormond.r: The earls ruled their palatinate from Kilkenny Castle, bought in 1391, and Carrick-on-Suir, with their own courts. Generally loyal to the crown, they were rivals of the Kildare and Desmond FitzGeralds. Thomas Butler, the 10th Earl, helped crush the Desmond rebellions; James Butler, 1st Duke of Ormonde, was Lord Lieutenant under Charles II.
earldom-of-ormond.e: James Butler, 2nd Duke, joined the Jacobites and was attainted in 1715, and the Tipperary palatinate was abolished in 1716. The Butlers kept Kilkenny Castle until 1967.

early-duchy-of-aquitaine.t: Independent duchy of south-western Gaul whose dukes defied the Franks and fought the Umayyad advance in the 8th century.
early-duchy-of-aquitaine.o: As Merovingian power weakened in the mid 7th century, the region south of the Loire came under semi-independent dukes. Felix, a nobleman of Toulouse, is recorded around 660, followed by Lupus and then Odo, called the Great, who ruled Aquitaine and Gascony from around 700.
early-duchy-of-aquitaine.r: The duchy kept a strong Gallo-Roman identity and Roman law. Odo defeated an Umayyad army besieging Toulouse in 721, one of the first checks on the Muslim advance, but was routed near Bordeaux in 732 and had to seek help from Charles Martel, joining him at the battle near Tours.
early-duchy-of-aquitaine.e: Odo's son Hunald and grandson Waiofar resisted the Carolingians, but Pippin the Short waged yearly wars against Waiofar until his murder in 768. A last rising under a second Hunald was crushed by Charlemagne in 769, and Aquitaine became part of the Kingdom of the Franks.

exarchate-of-ravenna.t: Byzantine province ruling what remained of imperial Italy from Ravenna, under an exarch combining military and civil power, until the Lombards took Ravenna in 751.
exarchate-of-ravenna.o: After the Lombard invasion of 568 broke Byzantine Italy into scattered territories, Emperor Maurice concentrated civil and military authority in a single governor, the exarch, based at Ravenna. The office is first attested in 584. It was a new form of government designed for a frontier under constant attack.
exarchate-of-ravenna.r: The exarch governed Ravenna, the Pentapolis, the Duchy of Rome, Naples, Venetia and other fragments, commanding local garrisons whose officers became a landed aristocracy. Relations with the popes were often tense, especially over Monothelitism and Iconoclasm. Several exarchs rebelled, among them Eleutherius in 619 and Olympius in 649. Ravenna remained a centre of Greek-Latin culture, its churches adorned with mosaics.
exarchate-of-ravenna.e: Lombard pressure grew in the 8th century; King Aistulf captured Ravenna in 751, killing or expelling the last exarch, Eutychius. When Pepin the Short defeated Aistulf, he gave the exarchate's lands to the pope in 756, forming the core of the Papal States.

epidii.t: People of Kintyre in western Scotland recorded by Ptolemy, whose name means 'horse people' and whose land later became the heart of Dál Riata.
epidii.o: Ptolemy's Geography of about 150 places the Epidii in the Kintyre peninsula and neighbouring islands of Argyll, with the Mull of Kintyre named Epidion Akron after them. Their name comes from the Brittonic word for horse, suggesting a people who honoured horses or a horse deity.
epidii.r: Nothing is known of their rulers or institutions. Kintyre and the islands were a land of duns, crannogs and small forts, with the sea as the main highway. The peninsula lies only about 20 kilometres from Antrim, and contact with Ireland was constant across the North Channel.
epidii.e: The Epidii disappear from the record after Ptolemy. By the 6th century their region was ruled by the Gaelic kings of Dál Riata, whose territory spanned Argyll and north Antrim, and Kintyre was held by its leading kindred, the Cenél nGabráin.

empire-of-nicaea.t: The largest Byzantine successor state after 1204, which rebuilt Byzantine power in Anatolia and recaptured Constantinople in 1261.
empire-of-nicaea.o: As the Fourth Crusade took Constantinople in 1204, Theodore Laskaris, son-in-law of Alexios III, gathered refugees and troops in Bithynia. With Nicaea as his base he fought off the Latins and the Seljuks, and in 1208 had himself crowned emperor by a newly elected patriarch, giving his state the strongest claim to Byzantine legitimacy.
empire-of-nicaea.r: The Laskarid emperors governed through a Byzantine-style court and bureaucracy, with the patriarch residing at Nicaea and the court often at Nymphaion. John III Vatatzes promoted agricultural self-sufficiency, restricted luxury imports, founded charities and expanded into Europe, taking Thessalonica in 1246. Scholarship flourished under Nikephoros Blemmydes and Theodore II Laskaris.
empire-of-nicaea.e: Michael VIII Palaiologos seized power from the boy emperor John IV, defeated the Latins and Epirotes at Pelagonia in 1259 and took Constantinople in July 1261, restoring the Byzantine Empire. Neglect of the Anatolian frontier after the move opened the way to Turkish expansion.

earldom-of-bamburgh.t: The English lordship that survived the Viking conquest of York, ruling northern Northumbria from the fortress of Bamburgh.
earldom-of-bamburgh.o: When the Great Heathen Army took York in 867, the northern part of the Kingdom of Northumbria between the Tees and the Tweed remained under English rulers based at Bamburgh. Its leaders, such as Eadwulf and his descendants, styled themselves high-reeves or even kings of the northern English.
earldom-of-bamburgh.r: Bamburgh's lords protected the community of Saint Cuthbert, which moved with its relics to Chester-le-Street and then Durham. They recognised West Saxon kings from Aethelstan onwards, while defending Lothian against Scottish attack. Uhtred the Bold defeated the Scots at Durham in 1006 and held the whole earldom of Northumbria.
earldom-of-bamburgh.e: Feuds and Danish rule weakened the house. In 1041 Earl Siward killed Eadwulf, the last of the line, and united Northumbria under his own authority as part of the Kingdom of England. Lothian had already passed to the Kingdom of Scotland.

earldom-of-desmond.t: The FitzGerald lordship of Munster that became more Gaelic than the Gaels, destroyed in the Desmond Rebellions of the 1570s and 1580s.
earldom-of-desmond.o: The FitzGeralds descended from Maurice FitzGerald, one of the first Cambro-Norman invaders of 1169. Maurice FitzThomas FitzGerald was created Earl of Desmond in 1329 with palatine rights over Kerry.
earldom-of-desmond.r: The Desmond earls ruled much of Munster from castles such as Askeaton and Newcastle West, adopting Irish language, law and patronage of poets. Gerald, the 3rd Earl, was a noted Irish poet. They were often at odds with the Butler earls of the Earldom of Ormond and with the Dublin government.
earldom-of-desmond.e: Gerald FitzGerald, the 15th Earl, rebelled against Elizabeth I in the Desmond Rebellions. He was killed in 1583, and his vast lands were confiscated and granted to English settlers in the Plantation of Munster.

edetani.t: An Iberian people of the Valencian plain, centred on Edeta near Llíria, whose leader Edeco was among the first to join Rome.
edetani.o: The Edetani occupied the coastal plain and hills of the modern province of Valencia, between the Júcar and the Mijares, from about the 5th century BCE. Their capital, Edeta, stood on the hill of Tossal de Sant Miquel above Llíria.
edetani.r: Edeta's excavated houses have yielded famous painted pottery showing warriors, dancers and hunting scenes, with Iberian inscriptions. The Edetani lived from farming, crafts and trade along the coast, and their leaders controlled networks of villages and watchtowers. In 209 BCE their prince Edeco went over to Scipio after the fall of Carthago Nova, recovering his family held hostage there.
edetani.e: The Edetani joined Rome during the Second Punic War and were absorbed into Hispania Citerior. In 138 BCE the Romans founded Valentia, modern Valencia, in their territory, and Edeta itself was later abandoned in favour of a Roman town on the plain.

electorate-of-bavaria.t: Bavaria as one of the great electoral principalities of the Empire, a Catholic power whose dukes twice sought the imperial crown.
electorate-of-bavaria.o: Duke Maximilian I, head of the Catholic League, helped crush the Bohemian revolt at the White Mountain in 1620. As a reward Emperor Ferdinand II transferred the electoral dignity of the Palatinate to him in 1623, together with the Upper Palatinate, confirmed at the Peace of Westphalia in 1648.
electorate-of-bavaria.r: The electorate was firmly Catholic, with strong ties to the Jesuits and a rich baroque church culture. The electors built Nymphenburg and Schleissheim palaces in and near Munich. Max Emanuel allied with France in the War of the Spanish Succession and lost his lands after Blenheim in 1704, and Charles Albert was elected Emperor Charles VII in 1742 during the Austrian Succession war.
electorate-of-bavaria.e: In 1777 the Bavarian Wittelsbachs died out and the electorate passed to Charles Theodore of the Palatinate. Allied with Napoleon, Elector Maximilian IV Joseph gained large territories and became King of Bavaria on 1 January 1806.

epirote-league.t: Federal republic of the peoples of Epirus that replaced the Aeacid monarchy and ended in mass enslavement by Rome in 167 BCE.
epirote-league.o: Around 232 BCE the last of the royal Aeacid family, Deidamia, was killed and the Molossians, Chaonians and Thesprotians abolished the monarchy of the Kingdom of Epirus. They formed a federal state, the Koinon of the Epirotes, whose meetings were often held at Phoenice in Chaonia, near the Ionian coast.
epirote-league.r: The league was led by annually elected generals and a federal assembly, and minted coins showing Zeus and Dione of Dodona. Its regions remained distinct, and wealth came from herding and trade with Italy. Illyrian raiders under Queen Teuta sacked Phoenice in 230 BCE. The Peace of Phoenice, ending the First Macedonian War in 205 BCE, was signed there.
epirote-league.e: In the Third Macedonian War the Molossians sided with Perseus while other Epirotes supported Rome. In 167 BCE the Roman Senate ordered Lucius Aemilius Paullus to punish Epirus: seventy towns were plundered and about 150,000 people enslaved, ending the league.
epirote-league.re: Ancient Greek religion (cult of Zeus at Dodona)

ezeritai.t: Slavic tribe of the lower Eurotas valley in Laconia, a tribute-paying neighbour of the Melingoi under Byzantine rule.
ezeritai.o: The Ezeritai, whose name probably comes from the Slavic word for lake, settled in the marshy plain of Helos in southern Laconia during the Slavic migrations into the Peloponnese of the late 6th and 7th centuries. They first appear clearly in Byzantine sources of the 9th and 10th centuries.
ezeritai.r: Like the Melingoi, the Ezeritai kept their own leaders and paid a fixed tribute instead of regular taxes, set by Constantine VII at 300 gold coins a year. They were subdued by Theoktistos Bryennios in the 840s and rebelled again in the 920s under Romanos I, after which their tribute was raised. Little else is recorded of their society.
ezeritai.e: They remained distinct under Frankish rule in the 13th century and are mentioned in the Chronicle of the Morea. Over time they converted to Orthodox Christianity and merged into the Greek population of Laconia, leaving place names as their main trace.
ezeritai.re: Slavic paganism, later Eastern Orthodox Christianity

euboean-league.t: Federation of the cities of Euboea, born from the island's revolt against Athens in 411 BCE and revived repeatedly under Macedonian and Roman patrons.
euboean-league.o: Euboea was vital to Athens, supplying food and pasture. In 411 BCE, after a Spartan naval victory off Eretria, its cities revolted and formed a league, building a bridge across the Euripus to link Chalcis with the mainland. Federal coins inscribed for the Euboeans appear from about this time.
euboean-league.r: The league joined Chalcis, Eretria, Histiaea and Carystus with a federal council and coinage, though the larger cities often pursued their own policies. Its history was one of shifting allegiances: members joined the Second Athenian League, while Callias of Chalcis revived the federation in the 340s BCE in a contest between Athens and Philip II for the island.
euboean-league.e: Under the Hellenistic kings, Chalcis was one of Macedon's 'fetters of Greece'. After Flamininus proclaimed the freedom of the Greeks in 196 BCE the league was refounded under Roman patronage. It lost its independence after the Achaean War of 146 BCE, when Chalcis was punished for supporting the Achaeans.

eleutherna.t: Hill city of western Crete on the slopes of Mount Ida whose Orthi Petra cemetery has revealed rich warrior burials of the early Iron Age.
eleutherna.o: Eleutherna occupied a long ridge on the north-west slopes of Mount Ida, inhabited since the Bronze Age. It grew into a city in the early Iron Age, and by the 7th century BCE it was one of the important poleis of Crete.
eleutherna.r: Excavations at the Orthi Petra necropolis since 1985 have found rich burials of the 9th to 7th centuries BCE, including warriors and elite women with gold jewellery. Like other Cretan cities, Eleutherna had kosmoi magistrates and aristocratic institutions. It minted coins showing Apollo and took part in Hellenistic alliances and the Cretan Koinon.
eleutherna.e: Metellus captured Eleutherna during the Roman conquest of Crete in 68 or 67 BCE. It continued as a Roman and early Byzantine town before being abandoned, probably after an earthquake in the 7th century CE.

esuvii.t: Little-known Gallic people of lower Normandy subdued by Caesar's legate Crassus during the conquest of Armorica.
esuvii.o: Caesar mentions the Esuvii among the Armorican peoples brought under Roman control by Publius Crassus in 57 BCE, and notes that a legion wintered in their territory in 54 BCE. Their exact location is debated, but most scholars place them in the Orne region around Sées or Exmes.
esuvii.r: Nothing is known of their rulers or institutions; their name may be linked to the Gallic god Esus.
esuvii.e: After the conquest they disappear from the record, and their land seems to have been absorbed into the civitas of the Sagii, whose town became Sées.

epidaurus.t: Argolid city-state whose sanctuary of Asclepius became the most famous healing centre of the Greek world, with its magnificent theatre.
epidaurus.o: Epidaurus lay on a small peninsula on the east coast of the Argolid. In the early Iron Age Dorian settlers from Argos made it an independent city; tradition held that Epidaurians in turn settled Aegina. Its sanctuary of Apollo Maleatas inland gradually gave way to the cult of his son Asclepius.
epidaurus.r: Epidaurus was governed by an oligarchy of 180 citizens. From the late 5th century BCE the Asclepieion attracted sick pilgrims who slept in the sanctuary hoping for healing dreams, and inscriptions record their cures. The 4th century BCE theatre, attributed to Polykleitos the Younger, seats about 13,000. Epidaurus was a loyal member of the Peloponnesian League.
epidaurus.e: Epidaurus joined the Achaean League in 243 BCE and passed under Rome in 146 BCE. Sulla plundered the sanctuary in 87 BCE, but it recovered and flourished in Roman times; its theatre still hosts performances.

elea.t: Greek city on the Cilento coast founded by refugees from Phocaea, home of the philosophers Parmenides and Zeno and of the Eleatic school.
elea.o: Around 540 BCE Phocaean Greeks, who had fled their city in Asia Minor before the Persians and then lost much of their fleet at the battle of Alalia off Corsica, founded Elea (later Roman Velia) on a headland south of Poseidonia with help from Rhegion.
elea.r: Elea lived by the sea: fishing, trade and shipping rather than farming, as its hilly territory was poor. It is best known for philosophy: Parmenides, said to have written the city's laws, and his pupil Zeno founded the Eleatic school, which shaped Greek thinking about being and change. The Porta Rosa, a 4th-century BCE arched gateway, is an early true arch in a Greek city. Elea resisted Lucanian pressure while other Greek cities fell.
elea.e: Elea allied with Rome in the early 3rd century BCE and supplied ships in the Punic Wars; Rome recruited priestesses of Ceres from Velia. It kept Greek speech and became a Roman municipium after 89 BCE. Silting of its harbour led to decline, and its remains are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

emirate-of-sicily.t: Muslim Sicily, ruled from Palermo for over two centuries, which transformed the island's farming, cities and language before the Norman conquest.
emirate-of-sicily.o: In 827 the Aghlabids of Ifriqiya invaded Sicily at the invitation of the rebel Byzantine commander Euphemius. Palermo fell in 831 and became the capital, but the conquest was slow: Syracuse fell in 878, Taormina in 902 and Rometta in 965. Malta was taken in 870.
emirate-of-sicily.r: After Fatimid takeover in 909, the Kalbid family ruled as emirs from 948, beginning with Hasan al-Kalbi. Palermo grew into one of the largest Mediterranean cities; Ibn Hawqal counted some 300 mosques. The Arabs introduced citrus, sugar cane, cotton and new irrigation techniques. Christians and Jews lived as protected subjects, and Siculo-Arabic, the ancestor of Maltese, spread widely.
emirate-of-sicily.e: From the 1040s the emirate split among rival lords. One of them, Ibn al-Thumna, invited the Normans, and Roger I took Messina in 1061 and Palermo in 1072; Noto, the last Muslim stronghold, fell in 1091. Arab-Norman culture flourished under the Norman kings.

eburones.t: Belgic people between the Meuse and the Rhine who destroyed a Roman legion in 54 BCE and were wiped out by Caesar in revenge.
eburones.o: The Eburones lived between the Meuse and the Rhine, in modern eastern Belgium and the southern Netherlands. Caesar counts them among the Germani Cisrhenani and says they had paid tribute to the Aduatuci.
eburones.r: They were ruled jointly by two kings, Ambiorix and the elderly Catuvolcus. Their stronghold was Atuatuca, where Caesar stationed troops for the winter of 54 BCE.
eburones.e: In 54 BCE Ambiorix lured the legion and a half under Sabinus and Cotta out of Atuatuca and destroyed it. In 53 BCE Caesar invited neighbouring peoples to plunder their land; Catuvolcus poisoned himself with yew, while Ambiorix escaped. Their territory was later settled by the Tungri.

emirate-of-crete.t: Muslim emirate founded by Andalusian exiles that held Crete for over a century and made it a base for raiding the Byzantine Aegean.
emirate-of-crete.o: After a failed revolt in Cordoba in 818, thousands of Andalusians were expelled from the Umayyad Emirate. Many reached Alexandria, which they held for some years before being forced out. Led by Abu Hafs Umar, they landed on Byzantine Crete in the 820s, conquered the island and founded a fortified capital, Chandax, on the site of modern Heraklion.
emirate-of-crete.r: The emirs ruled as a hereditary dynasty, nominally recognising the Abbasid caliphs, and Arabic and Islam spread among part of the population. The emirate grew rich from raiding Aegean coasts, the slave trade and commerce with Egypt and Syria, and minted its own coins. It repelled several Byzantine expeditions, including those of 843, 911 and 949.
emirate-of-crete.e: In 960 the general Nikephoros Phokas landed a great army and took Chandax after a winter siege in March 961. The last emir, Abd al-Aziz ibn Shu'ayb, was taken to Constantinople. Crete returned to Byzantium and was re-Christianised.

earldom-of-ulster.t: The Anglo-Norman lordship of eastern Ulster founded by John de Courcy and held by the de Burghs, whose collapse in 1333 opened the way to Gaelic recovery.
earldom-of-ulster.o: John de Courcy invaded Ulster in 1177 and ruled it from Carrickfergus and Downpatrick. In 1205 King John expelled him and created the earldom of Ulster for Hugh de Lacy. After de Lacy's death the earldom passed in 1263 to Walter de Burgh.
earldom-of-ulster.r: The earls held coastal Antrim and Down with castles, towns such as Carrickfergus and Coleraine, and manors worked by English settlers. Richard de Burgh, the Red Earl, was the most powerful lord in Ireland around 1300, overlord of the O'Neills and lord of much of Connacht. Edward Bruce's invasion of 1315 to 1318 devastated the earldom.
earldom-of-ulster.e: In 1333 William Donn de Burgh, the Brown Earl, was murdered at Carrickfergus. The earldom passed by marriage to the English royal family, but Gaelic lords such as the O'Neills of Clandeboye reoccupied most of its lands.

emirate-of-granada.t: The last Muslim state in Iberia, ruled by the Nasrid dynasty for over 250 years and builder of the Alhambra.
emirate-of-granada.o: In 1232 Muhammad ibn Yusuf ibn Nasr, known as Ibn al-Ahmar, proclaimed himself ruler at Arjona amid the collapse of Almohad power. He took Granada in 1237-1238 and in 1246 accepted vassalage to Ferdinand III of Castile, ceding Jaén and paying tribute to survive.
emirate-of-granada.r: The emirate covered the mountains and coasts from Almería to Gibraltar, dense with refugees from lost Andalusi cities. Silk, sugar and dried fruit were exported through Málaga, often by Genoese merchants. Yusuf I and Muhammad V built the finest parts of the Alhambra, and poets such as Ibn Zamrak and the vizier Ibn al-Khatib served the court.
emirate-of-granada.e: Weakened by dynastic feuds, Granada fell in the war of 1482-1492. Muhammad XII, Boabdil, surrendered the city to Isabella I and Ferdinand II on 2 January 1492. Its Muslims later faced forced conversion and, as Moriscos, expulsion.

eblani.t: People of eastern Ireland named in Ptolemy's Geography, whose town Eblana has often, though doubtfully, been linked with Dublin.
eblani.o: The Eblani are known only from the Geography of Ptolemy, compiled around 150 from earlier sailors' reports. He places them on the east coast of Ireland, south of the Voluntii and north of the Cauci, roughly in the area of modern County Dublin and Meath, with a town called Eblana.
eblani.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers, society or customs. The resemblance of Eblana to Dublin led older writers to identify the two, but most scholars now doubt the link, since Dublin's name is Irish and Ptolemy's coordinates are imprecise. Archaeology shows Roman goods reaching the east coast at sites such as Drumanagh.
eblani.e: The Eblani do not appear in any later source, and no Irish tradition preserves their name. Their area later fell within the territory of the Kingdom of Leinster and of the rising Uí Néill dynasties of Brega.

east-breifne.t: The O'Reilly lordship of County Cavan, a Gaelic state with its own coinage and a town at Cavan, until the Plantation of Ulster.
east-breifne.o: East Breifne emerged when the Kingdom of Breifne split in 1256 and the O'Reillys, Muintir Mhaoilmhordha, took the eastern part. They founded the town of Cavan around their castle at Clough Oughter and the Franciscan friary.
east-breifne.r: The O'Reillys traded with the Pale, and their 'O'Reilly money', clipped coins circulating in the 15th century, was common enough to be banned by the Irish Parliament in 1447. The lordship was organised in Gaelic fashion, with tanistry, brehon law and a hereditary learned class.
east-breifne.e: Under the Tudors the area became County Cavan in 1584. After the Nine Years' War and the Flight of the Earls it was included in the Plantation of Ulster from 1609, with lands granted to English and Scottish settlers.

elusates.t: Aquitanian people of the Armagnac whose town Elusa, modern Eauze, became a provincial capital of late Roman Gaul.
elusates.o: The Elusates lived in the north-west of the modern Gers, in the Armagnac hills. Caesar names them among the Aquitanian peoples who surrendered to Publius Crassus in 56 BCE.
elusates.r: Nothing is known of their pre-Roman government. They belonged to the Aquitani, whose language was related to Basque.
elusates.e: Under Rome Elusa grew into a prosperous town, and in the late 3rd century it became the capital of the province of Novempopulana. The Eauze treasure, a hoard of nearly 28,000 coins and jewellery buried in the 3rd century, shows its wealth.

electorate-of-mainz.t: The most powerful church state of the Holy Roman Empire, whose archbishop was arch-chancellor of Germany and convened the elections of kings.
electorate-of-mainz.o: The see of Mainz was raised to an archbishopric around 780 to 782, building on the work of Saint Boniface, archbishop there from 746. Its province became the largest in Latin Christendom. Royal grants from the Ottonians onwards gave the archbishops temporal lordship over Mainz and scattered lands along the Main, the Rhine, in Hesse and the Eichsfeld.
electorate-of-mainz.r: From 965 the archbishop held the title of arch-chancellor of Germany, and the Golden Bull of 1356 confirmed him as first among the seven prince-electors, presiding over imperial elections. Mainz was governed by its cathedral chapter and archbishop. Gutenberg invented printing there in the 1450s, and the university was founded in 1477.
electorate-of-mainz.e: France occupied the left bank of the Rhine during the Revolutionary Wars, and the short-lived Republic of Mainz was proclaimed in 1793. The Reichsdeputationshauptschluss of 1803 dissolved the electorate; its last elector, Karl Theodor von Dalberg, kept a state centred on Aschaffenburg and Regensburg.

emirate-of-cordoba.t: The independent Umayyad state in al-Andalus founded by a refugee prince in 756, which built the Great Mosque of Córdoba.
emirate-of-cordoba.o: After the Abbasids massacred the Umayyad family in 750, the prince Abd al-Rahman escaped to North Africa and crossed to al-Andalus in 755. Backed by Umayyad clients and Syrian troops, he defeated the governor Yusuf al-Fihri in 756 and became emir at Córdoba, independent of Baghdad.
emirate-of-cordoba.r: The emirs built a centralised state with a professional army, a bureaucracy and a coinage. Abd al-Rahman I began the Great Mosque in 785. Al-Hakam I crushed the revolt of the suburb of Córdoba in 818, and Abd al-Rahman II, patron of the musician Ziryab, brought eastern fashions and repelled the Vikings from Seville in 844. Christians were steadily Arabised and converted.
emirate-of-cordoba.e: From the 880s revolts by muwallads such as Umar ibn Hafsun and local lords split the emirate. Abd al-Rahman III restored control from 912 and in 929 declared himself caliph, turning the emirate into the Caliphate of Córdoba.
